event: Elsie wakes at dawn to the grey glove on the sill by Moonpenny, and says good morning to both.
prose: Elsie woke to bread. The smell came up through the floorboards the way it did every morning from four, warm and brown, and lay over the attic like a second blanket. The round window was grey with dawn. Mist stood on Thimble Canal, so thick that only the tops of the lanterns showed above it, unlit, floating like paper boats. On the sill, where she had left it, the grey glove sat beside Moonpenny's clay pot with its fingers curled. It had kept its shape in the night. It looked like a hand resting on the sill, waiting for someone to take it. Elsie rolled over in the narrow bed and smiled at the two of them. "Good morning, Moonpenny." She thought about it. "Good morning, glove."

event: She waters the crate, Mrs Pennywhistle to Doris, and tells Moonpenny she's taking Noor cakes.
prose: She filled the chipped jug at the basin and went along the crate barefoot on the warm boards. Mrs Pennywhistle got a long drink, because ferns were thirsty things and she had been looking droopy at the tips. Sunny got hers at the roots, round the little green lemon that wasn't growing any faster for being looked at. Captain got a splash and smelled of mint for it. Doris got a dribble, which was all an aloe ever wanted. Moonpenny came last. Elsie tipped the jug very carefully into her pot and knelt with her chin on the sill. "I'm taking Noor her cakes today. The ones with the raincloud. She'll say she isn't hungry. But everyone's hungry for honey cakes. You'll see."

memory.fact: Elsie's plants are Mrs Pennywhistle the fern, Sunny the lemon, Doris the aloe and Captain the mint.
Elsie's plants are Mrs Pennywhistle the fern, Sunny the lemon, Doris the aloe and Captain the mint.

event: She dresses, re-knots the snapped bootlace tighter, and tucks Noor's parcel into her satchel.
prose: She dressed: the cream halter, laced up the front and tied in a bow at the top, the sage skirt, the belt with its pouches, the fingerless gloves. She sat on the end of the bed to pull on her boots and looked at yesterday's bow on the left one, the fat floppy knot she'd tied on the guild steps with the two snapped ends. It had come half undone already. She untied it and tied it again, tighter, a hard little knot right down against the eyelet, and pulled until the lace bit her fingers. She stamped. It held. She put Noor's parcel into her satchel last, flat on top of the bandage rolls so it wouldn't squash, with the raincloud facing up, so she would see it every time she opened the flap.

event: She packs the second glove too, still only a cuff on its needles.
prose: She took the second glove off the table too. It was still only a cuff, a short grey ring of ribbing on its needles, two plain and two purl, with the ball of wool tucked inside it. She looked from it to the finished one on the sill. They didn't look like a pair yet. They looked like a hand and a bracelet. She wound the loose wool round the needles so the stitches couldn't slide off, and slipped it into the satchel beside the parcel. There would be walking today, probably. There usually was. She could do a great deal of cuff on a road. At the door she turned and looked back at the glove on the sill, and at Moonpenny beside it. She went down the narrow stairs.

event: Downstairs Agnes is shaking out a flour sack and frowning at the grit in the bottom of it.
prose: Downstairs the shop was all warmth and flour dust. The first loaves were out on the racks, and the shutters were still up, so the light came in only round their edges. Mrs Merriweather was at the back door with an empty flour sack held up by its corners. She was shaking it out over the yard step, the way she shook out every sack, so as not to waste the last of it. A soft white cloud went up off it into the grey morning. Something pattered on the stone, small and hard, like dropped seed. Mrs Merriweather stopped shaking. She turned the sack inside out and looked into the bottom seam, and frowned. She picked something out of the seam with her thumbnail and held it up to the light. It was grit.

event: Agnes says Hobb Mill's flour has come short and gritty all month, and Bess Hobb is behind.
prose: "Hobb Mill." It was more than Mrs Merriweather usually said before breakfast. She rubbed the grit between her finger and thumb, and it squeaked. "That's their flour. Short in the sack all month, and gritty, and late." She folded the sack in four, very square, and laid it on the pile by the door. "Bess Hobb's not late. Not in twenty years. Her mother before her wasn't either." She went back to the big table and dusted her hands on her apron and looked at the grit still on her thumb. "She's behind. Something's wrong out there." She wiped the thumb on her apron and didn't say any more about it.

memory.fact: All month Hobb Mill's flour has come to the Honeycomb short in the sack, gritty and late.
All month Hobb Mill's flour has come to the Honeycomb short in the sack, gritty and late.

event: Agnes says a girl with long braids stood at the window last night, a good while, and didn't knock.
prose: She took up her bread paddle. She didn't look up from the loaves. "There was a girl at the window last night." Elsie stopped with her hand on the stair rail. "After you'd gone up. Late. A girl with her hair in long braids, down to here." She touched the middle of her own back with the end of the paddle. "Stood out on the canal walk and looked at your plate a good while. Under the lantern. I saw her from the back room." She slid the paddle under a loaf. "Didn't knock. Stood a long time, and then went off toward the bridge."

memory.fact: A girl with long braids stood long at the Honeycomb window, looking at the honey cakes.
A girl with long braids stood long at the Honeycomb window, looking at the honey cakes.
A girl with long braids stood long at the Honeycomb window, looking at the honey cakes.

event: Elsie claps her hands and says she came, and her eyes fill, and Agnes hands her a cloth.
prose: Elsie clapped her hands. The clap went off in the warm shop like a cork. "She came! Oh, Mrs Merriweather. She came." She could see it: the canal walk under the red lantern, and Amara standing there in the dark with her braids down her back, looking at the honey cakes on the blue plate, being nobody in particular. The shop went blurry. Her eyes had filled all at once, the way they did, and a tear ran down beside her nose before she could catch it. Mrs Merriweather looked at her. She reached under the counter without a word and brought out a clean cloth, folded in four, and held it out across the bread. Elsie took it and laughed into it and wiped her eyes.

event: Elsie leaves the honey cakes in the window another day, in case, and Agnes lets her.
prose: The honey cakes were still on their blue plate in the window, in their row. They had gone a little dull overnight, and the crust had softened. Elsie went and stood over them with the cloth still in her hand. "Can they stay? Another day? In case she comes back. She might be braver tonight." Mrs Merriweather looked at the plate, and at the window, and at Elsie. She was quiet long enough that Elsie began to think about the space the plate took up, where the morning rolls should go. At last Mrs Merriweather moved the tray of rolls to the other end of the window and squared it. "They'll go stale." That was all. The plate stayed where it was.

event: Tamsin knocks at the shop door early, Margery on her shoulder, yawning, curls still damp.
prose: At seven there was a knock on the shop door, the hard double knock of a fist that didn't think much about knocking. Elsie opened it. Tamsin stood on the step in the mist with Margery over one shoulder and her mouth wide open in a yawn so big her eyes watered. Her copper curls were dark and damp, still wet from a wash, and pushed back off her face anyhow. Drops ran down her neck into her jerkin. She finished the yawn and grinned. "Told you. Early." Behind her Thimble Canal was still white, and the lanterns hung in the mist with only their tops showing.

event: Elsie gives her a honey cake off the plate; Tamsin eats it in two bites and licks her thumb.
prose: Elsie took a honey cake off the blue plate. There were so many, and Amara wouldn't mind one. She held it out. Tamsin looked at it, and at the plate in the window, and took it. She ate it in two bites, standing on the step, the first bite half the cake and the second bite the rest, and chewed with her eyes shut. She licked the honey off her thumb, slowly, all the way round, and opened her eyes. Her mouth was still full. "That beats porridge." She swallowed. "Was that breakfast? I'm counting it as breakfast."

event: Elsie tells Tamsin about the girl with braids; Tamsin says Amara will come when she's brave enough.
prose:
"Tamsin, Amara came! Last night, late, after I'd gone up. Mrs Merriweather saw her. A girl with long braids, under the lantern, looking at the plate. And she stood there ever so long." It all came out on the step in a rush.

Tamsin listened with her head on one side. She didn't laugh. When Elsie had finished she looked past her at the window, at the plate, and nodded slowly. "She'll come in. When she's brave enough. Takes a while, that kind of brave." She rubbed her damp curls with the flat of her hand. "Took me a year to walk up a plank to my own mum's barge. And I'm brave as a bull." She hitched Margery higher. "She'll come."

memory.fact: A girl with long braids stood long at the Honeycomb window, looking at the honey cakes.

event: They walk along Thimble Canal toward Brightwater Square in the mist coming off the water.
prose: They walked along Thimble Canal toward Brightwater Square. The mist was coming off the water in slow white curls. It hung under the arched bridges and crept up their steps. The lanterns along the bank swung in it, wet, dripping from their paper. Boats went by unseen, a pole knocking, a voice calling. Elsie's breath showed. She walked close to Tamsin for the warmth, and Tamsin let her, and their arms bumped as they went. A heron stood on a mooring post, grey in the grey, and kept quite still as they passed. Tamsin glared at it. "That heron owes me money." Elsie laughed so loud it came back to her from under the next bridge.

event: At a coffee stall on the square Elsie buys a cup of black coffee, strong, nothing in it: two pips.
prose: Brightwater Square was waking up. The guild hall's copper roof showed green above the mist. Under the plane trees at the edge of the square a woman had a coffee stall going, a brazier and a big black pot and a row of thick clay cups. The smell came across the cobbles, bitter and dark. Elsie went straight to it. "A cup of black coffee, please. Strong. With nothing in it." The woman poured it from the pot, black as the canal at night. Elsie counted two copper pips out of her pouch into her palm and handed them over. The cup was so hot she had to hold it by the rim.

changes.note: Elsie buys Noor a cup of black coffee on Brightwater Square: 2 pips, 187 → 185

event: Tamsin asks who drinks that muck; Elsie says it's in her book, under the raincloud.
prose:
Tamsin looked into the cup and made a face. "Who drinks that muck? Looks like tar. Smells like a burnt boot."

Elsie held it carefully in front of her in both hands, walking slowly so it wouldn't slop. "Noor does. It's in my book. Black coffee, strong, nothing in it." She pointed with her chin, since her hands were full, at the satchel on her hip. "Under the raincloud."

Tamsin looked at her sideways for a long moment. At last she shook her head and grinned at the cobbles. "Under the raincloud. Course it is."

event: Tilly is sitting on the guild steps with a fat book of grave things open on her knees.
prose: Tilly was sitting on the guild steps. She was hunched over a book so fat it lay across both her knees and still hung over the sides, a brown old book with a cracked spine and grave things stamped on it in faded gold. Her goggles were pushed up and her braids were over her shoulders. There was a pencil behind her ear and another in her mouth. She was reading with her finger. As they came up she lifted her head with the pencil still in her teeth, and her eyes were pink at the rims and enormous. She took the pencil out. "Elsie! Tamsin. You've got to hear this."

event: Tilly says she read till two and knows nine ways to stop a wight, and is very sorry for the wight.
prose: "I read till two." She turned the book round to show them a page of very small print and a woodcut of something tall and thin standing in a doorway. "I know nine ways to stop a wight now. Nine. Lamplight, which we knew. Salt. Running water. Iron, but it has to be cold iron. A bell. Its true name, if you've got it, which you won't have. And three I can't say before breakfast." She shut the book on her finger, and her face went sorry. "And it's so sad, Elsie. They're only guarding. It says so. They were put there to guard the dead, and they're still there, hundreds of years on, guarding." She sniffed. "I'm very sorry for the wight."

memory.fact: Tilly's book of grave things gives nine ways to stop a wight, among them salt, cold iron and a bell.

event: Inside, Cora stands by the clerk's desk, ledger under her arm; the harebell is gone from her coat.
prose: Inside, the guild hall was filling up, and it smelled of last night's ale and this morning's sawdust. The lamps were out. Grey light came down from the high windows. Cora was standing by the clerk's desk with her ledger under her arm, already there, already buttoned to the throat, as though she'd been standing in that spot since the doors opened. Elsie went across to her, smiling, with the coffee held out in front of her. Halfway there she looked at Cora's coat. The top buttonhole was empty. The harebell was gone. There was only the buttonhole, a small neat slit in the charcoal cloth, with nothing in it.

event: Elsie asks after it; Cora says it wilted, so she pressed it, then looks sorry she said so.
prose:
"Cora! Your harebell."

Cora's hand went up to the buttonhole and found it empty, as though she'd forgotten. "It wilted. Yesterday. They don't last, picked." She paused. "So I pressed it. In a book. Flat, under the—" She stopped. Her mouth shut. A faint colour came up out of her collar, and she looked at the desk, at the clerk's inkwell, at the board, anywhere but at Elsie.

Elsie beamed up at her. "Oh, good. Then you've still got it."

changes.note: Bond: Cora 43 → 45 (confidence: she pressed the harebell)

memory.fact: When Elsie's harebell wilted, Cora pressed it flat in a book.

event: Elsie asks if Cora slept; Cora says yes, and Elsie sees the grey under her eyes and doubts it.
prose:
Elsie looked up at her. "Did you sleep?"

Cora's grey eyes came back from the board. "Yes." It came at once, very crisp, the way things came for the ledger. Elsie looked at her face. The grey smudges were still under her eyes, the same ones as at the barrow, darker if anything, like thumbprints in ash. The skin there looked thin. Her bun was perfect. Her coat was perfect. Her eyes weren't. Elsie looked at the smudges for a while and didn't say anything, and didn't believe her, not even a little.

event: Cora says the guildmaster read the barrow report, and asked nothing about the empty name.
prose: Cora shifted the ledger under her arm and spoke in her report voice, to a point somewhere over Elsie's head. "The guildmaster read my report. Last night, before she went home. Both sheets." She paused. "She signed it. She asked about the lights, and the wight, and the shepherd's hurdle." Another pause, longer. "She didn't ask about the name. The empty line. She read it. I watched her read it. She put her finger on it." She looked down at Elsie then. "And then she turned the page, and didn't ask a thing."

memory.fact: The guildmaster signed Cora's barrow report and asked nothing about its empty name line.
The guildmaster signed Cora's barrow report and asked nothing about its empty name line.

event: Noor sits alone in her ring of empty tables, a cup in her gloved hand, eyes on the door.
prose: Elsie looked past her, down the hall, to the corner under the Leftovers. Noor was there. She sat at the same table as yesterday, alone, very straight, in her long green coat. The three tables round her stood empty in their ring with the benches pushed in, though men were standing at the bar for want of room. She had a cup in one gloved hand. She wasn't drinking from it. Her eyes were on the big front door of the hall, and they stayed on it while Elsie watched, dark and steady under the kohl. At last they moved. They found Elsie by the clerk's desk and stopped there.

event: Elsie crosses the ring with the coffee, catches her toe on nothing, and pitches forward.
prose: Elsie went to her. She crossed the hall with the coffee held out in both hands, past the crowded benches and over the line where the crowd stopped, out into the ring of empty tables. The floor there was swept and bare, like a dance floor before a dance. She smiled at Noor across it. She was three tables away when her right toe caught. She looked afterward, and there was only floorboard, flat and smooth, not so much as a raised nail. But her toe caught on it all the same, and her foot stopped, and the rest of her went on. She pitched forward with her arms out, and the cup flew up out of her hands.

event: Tamsin's hand shoots past her, plucks the cup out of the air, and hands it back to her, full.
prose: Something went past her ear in a rush of air. It was Tamsin's arm. Tamsin had been two steps behind her, and now she was beside her. Her hand shot out past Elsie's head and closed round the cup in the air, as neatly as a hand closing on a thrown apple. The coffee slopped up to the brim and hung there, trembling, and sank back, every drop of it still in the cup. Elsie caught herself on the edge of a table with both hands flat. Tamsin stood holding the cup up at shoulder height, looking at it. "Ha!" She grinned at it. She put it back into Elsie's hands, full to the brim. "Your tar."

event: Elsie sets the coffee in front of Noor: black, strong, nothing in it, like her book says.
prose: Elsie straightened her skirt, the cup safe in both hands. She carried it the last three tables very carefully, looking at her feet the whole way. She set it down on Noor's table, in front of her, beside the cup Noor already had, and turned it so the handle faced Noor's gloved hand. "Black coffee. Strong. Nothing in it." She was a little out of breath. "Like your book says. My book. Your page of it." She smiled. "Good morning."

event: Noor looks at the cup a long time, then wraps both gloved hands round it and drinks.
prose: Noor looked at the cup. She looked at it for a long time, long enough that the steam stopped curling off it quite so high. Her face didn't move. Her eyes went from the coffee to Elsie and back to the coffee. At last she let go of the cup she'd had and pushed it aside. She put both her hands round the new one. The black gloves went right round it, the long fingers overlapping. She lifted it and drank, a long swallow, with her eyes shut. When she set it down her eyes stayed shut a moment longer.

memory.fact: Elsie brought Noor a cup of black coffee, strong, nothing in it, and Noor drank it.

event: Elsie tests the chair with both hands before sitting; it holds, and she beams.
prose: There was a chair across from Noor. Elsie looked at it. She took hold of its back in both hands and gave it a shake, a good hard one, and then leaned on the seat with her whole weight through her arms, the way you'd test a branch before you climbed it. She looked under it at the legs. She knocked on the seat with her knuckles, for luck. She sat down on it slowly, an inch at a time, ready to jump. It held. It didn't so much as creak. Elsie settled onto it squarely and beamed across the table at Noor, as proud as if she'd built the chair herself.

event: She sets the brown parcel by the cup; Noor reads her own name on it, and the little raincloud.
prose: She opened her satchel and took out the parcel. It had come through the morning flat and whole, the brown paper still folded the way Mrs Merriweather folded loaves. She set it on the table beside the coffee. Noor looked down at it. Elsie watched her read it: her own name, upside down to her, in Elsie's round pencil hand. Noor. Noor's eyes went sideways, to the little raincloud beside the name, the fat cloud with its six lines of rain. Her lips came a little apart. Her eyes stayed on the cloud.

changes.note: Bond: Noor 2 → 3 (kindness: black coffee and honey cakes, as her book says)

event: Noor asks what it is; Elsie says honey cakes, she made them, the crust is a baker's trick.
prose:
"What is it?" Noor's voice was low and very careful, as if the parcel might go off.

"Honey cakes. I made them. Last night, in the big oven downstairs." Elsie leaned forward, pleased. "The crust's a trick. The baker showed me. You brush them with the last of the honey when they come out, and put them back in while you count twenty. So they crackle." She tapped the paper with one finger. "There are four. You don't have to eat them all at once." She considered. "You can, though."

memory.fact: Agnes taught Elsie to brush her honey cakes with the last of the comb for a crust.
Agnes taught Elsie to brush her honey cakes with the last of the comb for a crust.

event: Noor doesn't open it; she slips it inside her coat, against her chest, and buttons the coat over it.
prose: Noor didn't open it. She looked at it a while longer. At last she picked it up in both gloved hands, carefully, by the edges. She unbuttoned the top two buttons of her green coat and slid the parcel inside, flat, against her chest, the way someone carries a letter she doesn't want to get wet. She did the buttons up again over it, one, two, and smoothed the coat down with her palm. Her hand stayed there a moment, flat on the green cloth, over the parcel. She picked up her coffee again.

memory.fact: Noor buttoned Elsie's parcel of honey cakes inside her coat, unopened.

event: Elsie's flower clip springs out of her hair and lands in Noor's lap.
prose: There was a small sharp click by Elsie's ear. Something sprang out of her hair. She felt it go, a little tug and then a lightness on one side of her head, and her hair fell forward across her eye. The flower clip went up in a little arc over the table, pink and white, turning over and over. It came down in Noor's lap, on the green coat. Elsie put her hand up to her hair. It was all loose on that side. "Oh!" She began to laugh. "It's jumped. It's not done that before." She pushed her hair out of her eye. "Your luck likes it."

changes.note: Elsie's flower clip springs out of her hair into Noor's lap

event: Noor picks it up in two gloved fingers and holds it out; Elsie asks her to put it back in, please.
prose: Noor looked down into her lap. She picked the clip up between two gloved fingers, the way you'd pick up a moth, and held it out across the table at arm's length. Her face had gone very still. Elsie looked at the clip, and at the black glove holding it. She didn't take it. She leaned forward over the table instead, and turned her head, and offered Noor the loose side of her hair. "Would you put it back in? Please? I can't see to do it. It goes in crooked without a mirror."

event: Noor leans across and clips it in above Elsie's ear, gloved fingers slow in her hair.
prose: For a moment Noor didn't move. At last she rose a little out of her chair and leaned across the table. Elsie felt her come close. She felt the gloved fingers touch her hair above her ear, and slip into it. They went in slowly. They gathered up the loose pink strands a few at a time, the leather cool and smooth against her scalp, and smoothed them back over her ear. Elsie shut her eyes. It was lovely, like having her hair brushed when she was small. The fingers held the hair in place. Last came the little cold press of the clip, and the click of it shutting, just where it belonged.

changes.note: Noor clips the flower clip back in above Elsie's ear

memory.fact: Noor clipped Elsie's flower clip back into her hair with her gloved fingers.

event: Noor's breath is close and uneven, and her fingers stay at Elsie's temple a moment too long.
prose: Noor didn't move back. She was very close. Elsie could hear her breathing just above her, and it wasn't even. It came short, and caught, and came short again, as if Noor had run up the guild steps. It was warm on Elsie's temple and smelled of black coffee. The gloved fingers stayed where they were. They rested at Elsie's temple, light, barely touching, after the clip was in and there was nothing left for them to do. They stayed there a moment too long. Through the thin leather Elsie could feel them trembling, very slightly. She smiled with her eyes shut and thought how kind Noor's hands were, and how careful.

event: She sits back fast, eyes on her cup, and her ears have gone pink under the black hair.
prose: Noor sat back, fast, all at once, and her chair scraped. Elsie opened her eyes. Noor had both hands round her cup again and her eyes down in it, on the black coffee, as if there were something written at the bottom that she had to read. Her face was perfectly still. But her ears had gone pink. They showed through the black hair where it fell straight past them, two little tips of pink, nearly as pink as Elsie's own hair. Elsie touched the clip. It was straight. "Thank you. It's perfect. You're much better at it than I am."

event: Elsie says she can't sit long today: there's a notice. So she brought lunch to Noor instead.
prose: She sighed, and looked over her shoulder at the board, where Tamsin was standing reading. "I can't sit long today. I'm sorry. There's a notice. Tamsin's looking for one now." She turned back. "And I said I'd sit here every day until you said yes to lunch. So I thought—" She pointed at Noor's coat, at the place over her chest where the parcel was. "I brought the lunch to you instead. So it still counts. It's still lunch with me. Only I won't be here for it." She thought about that. "I'm here for the beginning of it."

event: Noor says, dryly, that this is cheating; Elsie says it isn't, she'll be back tomorrow.
prose:
Noor looked at her over the cup. "That is cheating." It came out very dry, dry as old paper, and the corner of her mouth went in, hard, as if she were biting it.

"It isn't. It's honey cakes. You can't cheat with honey cakes." Elsie sat up straight on her good chair. "And I'll be back tomorrow. With my tea. And a chair I've shaken first." She nodded firmly. "So it's not cheating. It's only the first of a lot of days."

event: Cora comes into the ring and stops at the table; she and Noor look at each other, both very still.
prose: Someone stopped by the table. Elsie looked up. It was Cora. She had come across the empty ring after Elsie, straight-backed, with her ledger under her arm, and stopped at the edge of the table, and now she stood looking down at Noor. Noor had looked up at her. They both kept quiet. They both kept very still. Cora's face had gone to its stillest, the face she wore for reports, and Noor's had gone exactly the same. They looked at each other across the coffee cups like two cats meeting on a narrow wall. Elsie looked from one to the other.

event: Elsie asks, delighted, if they know each other; Noor says no, not to speak to.
prose:
"Oh!" Elsie clasped her hands together. "Do you know each other? Oh, how lovely, if you were friends already. Then I could have you both at once."

Noor's eyes went from Cora's face to Elsie's. "No." She drank some coffee. "Not to speak to."

event: Noor says the Warden has the rooms over hers on Wick Lane; on the stair they nod, and that is all.
prose: "She has the rooms over mine." She tipped her head a fraction toward Cora without looking at her. "The Warden. On Wick Lane, over the chandler's. I have the floor below." She turned her cup a quarter turn. "We pass on the stair. She nods. I nod." She said it to the coffee. "That's all of it."

event: Noor adds that the Warden walks the floor at night, and came in past eleven last night.
prose: "She walks the floor at night." Noor's voice was perfectly level. "Up and down. I hear her through my ceiling. Six steps to the window and six back, over and over." She drank. "And she came in past eleven last night. I heard her on the stair."

event: Cora goes red to the collar; Elsie asks, worried, if her bed is lumpy, and pats her arm.
prose: Cora went red. It started at her collar, above the top button, and climbed her neck and into her face, right up to the black of her hair, a slow deep red like a lantern being lit behind paper. Her mouth shut tight. She looked hard at the board. Elsie looked at her red face and was sorry for her, being talked about like that. She reached out and patted Cora's arm, twice, through the charcoal sleeve. "Cora, is your bed lumpy? Is that why you walk about?" She patted again. "You could fold a blanket under the bad part. That's what we did in the caravan, when the straw went flat."

event: Tamsin, at the board, calls out the E-rank notice: a boggart fouling the wheel at Hobb Mill.
prose: "Oi!" Tamsin's voice came down the hall from the board, loud enough to turn heads at the bar. She was standing at the E-rank end with a notice pulled half off its pin, reading it at arm's length. "Elsie! Here's one. Listen." She read it out. "Boggart fouling the wheel at Hobb Mill. Two hours south, on the Wend. Wheel jammed nightly." She looked round at them over her shoulder. "E-rank. Nine lanterns. That'll do us."

event: Elsie says Hobb Mill grinds Agnes's flour, so that settles it; Tilly sighs: not a grave thing.
prose:
"Hobb Mill!" Elsie stood up so fast her chair rocked, and she caught it. "That's Mrs Merriweather's mill. That's where her flour comes from. She said so this morning. It's coming short, and gritty, and Bess Hobb is behind." She looked at Noor, and at Cora, as if they must see it too. "So that settles it."

Tilly had come in from the steps and was standing at Tamsin's elbow with her fat book hugged to her chest. She looked at the notice over Tamsin's arm. She sighed, a long sigh, all the way down. "A boggart. That's not even a grave thing."

event: Noor tells Elsie, not quite lightly, to mind her head out there.
prose: Noor had been looking at her coffee. Now she looked up at Elsie, standing there with both hands on the chair back. "Elsie." The name came slowly, as though it were new in her mouth and she was trying the weight of it. "Mind your head out there." Her voice was light. But her eyes stayed on Elsie's face the whole time, and her gloved hand had tightened on the cup, and Elsie saw the black leather go taut over the knuckles.

event: At the clerk's desk Tamsin signs the party for the notice: nine lanterns; Cora writes in her ledger.
prose: At the clerk's desk Tamsin laid the notice down flat and signed for the party in her big square hand: Reyes, Brandt, Fairweather. The clerk read it, and looked at Elsie's name, and at Cora standing behind them. She stamped it. Nine lanterns, the notice said, on Hobb Mill's word that it was done. Cora had her ledger open on her arm. She wrote in it standing, the pen moving small and quick. Elsie leaned to see. Hobb Mill, it said, in Cora's exact hand, and the date, and the hour: twenty to nine. Elsie liked watching her write. Her hand stayed perfectly steady, even standing up.

event: Elsie waves to Noor from the door; Noor lifts her hand higher than yesterday.
prose: At the big door Elsie turned round. Noor was watching them go, the same as yesterday, from the middle of her ring of empty tables, with both hands round the coffee and the parcel buttoned inside her coat. Elsie put her arm up and waved, a big wave over her head, back and forth. Noor lifted her hand off the cup. She lifted it higher than yesterday. Yesterday it had come up off the table and stopped. Today it came up past her shoulder, the black glove open, and stayed there, up, while Elsie went out.

event: They go out by the south gate onto the river road beside the Wend.
prose: They went out by the south gate at twenty past nine, onto the river road. The mist had burned off. The sun was up and warm. The Wend ran beside the road, brown and quick, talking to itself over its stones. Willows leaned out over it. There were cows in the water meadows on the far side, standing knee-deep, and a kingfisher went past low over the water in a flick of blue. The road was dry and white with dust. Tamsin walked in front, swinging Margery. Tilly walked behind with her book open, reading as she went, and bumping into Tamsin's back whenever Tamsin stopped.

event: Elsie knits the second glove as she walks; the cuff grows, two plain, two purl.
prose: Elsie got out the second glove. She found the end of the wool and her place on the needles, and began. Two plain, two purl. Two plain, two purl. The needles clicked in time with her boots. The cuff went round and round in her hands and grew, a ring at a time, grey as the river in the shade of the willows. She could do it without looking, the way she'd done it behind the caravan for years, so she looked at the river instead, and the cows, and the long white road. She hummed a little without knowing she was humming. The cuff grew.

memory.fact: Now and then Elsie hums without knowing it.

event: Cora walks at her side watching the needles, and asks nothing this time.
prose: Cora walked at her side. She had her ledger under one arm and her other hand at her back, and she was watching the needles. Elsie could feel her watching. She watched the way she'd watched them yesterday on the downs, steadily, a long time, her grey eyes on the grey wool going round. Yesterday she had asked who they were for. Elsie waited, a little pleased with herself, ready to say surprise again. But today Cora didn't ask. She walked, and watched the needles going in and out, two plain, two purl, and kept her mouth closed. The road went on beside the river.

event: Cora reads out the notice she copied: a boggart fouling the wheel at Hobb Mill, to be removed.
prose: After a mile Cora took a folded paper out of the back of her ledger. "The notice. I copied it at the desk." She unfolded it and read it aloud in her reading voice, which was exactly like her report voice, only slower. "Hobb Mill, on the Wend, two hours south. A boggart is fouling the wheel. The race is choked each night with weed and stones. The wheel will not turn. The miller asks the guild to remove the boggart. Nine lanterns." She folded it again along its crease. "To be removed."

event: Elsie says the notice wants the wheel mended, not the boggart gone, and Cora writes that down.
prose: Elsie knitted to the end of a round, thinking. "But that's not what she wants." Cora looked at her. "Mrs Hobb. She doesn't want the boggart gone for its own sake. She wants her wheel to turn. Listen to it. The wheel won't turn, the race is choked. That's all wheel. The boggart's just who's doing it." She held up her knitting and pointed with a needle. "So the notice wants the wheel mended. That's the job, really." Cora looked at her a moment longer. At last she opened her ledger on her arm, walking, and wrote it down.

event: They reach Hobb Mill: tall stone, a great wooden wheel standing still, a willow, a thatched cottage.
prose: They came round a bend of the river at twenty past eleven, and there was the mill. It stood on the bank where the Wend ran narrow, tall and grey and square, built of river stone, with small deep windows high up and a hoist arm jutting out under the roof. Beside it was the wheel. It was enormous, taller than the mill door, dark wet wood with its paddles all round it, and it stood quite still. The water went past it choked and sulky. A great weeping willow trailed its hair in the river. Behind, in a garden full of beans, was a cottage with a thatched roof, low and golden, with smoke going up from the chimney.

event: Bess Hobb, stout, floury, meets them with her two grown daughters and says the race is choked again.
prose: A woman came out of the mill door to meet them, wiping her hands. She was stout and square, in a sacking apron, floury to the elbows, with flour in the lines of her face and in her greying hair, so that she looked dusted all over like a loaf. Two young women came out after her, one tall and one short, both floury, both with her square chin. "Guild?" She looked at Tamsin's axe and seemed comforted by it. "I'm Bess Hobb. These are my girls." She jerked her thumb at the wheel. "Race is choked again. Same as every night this month. Come and look."

event: The wheel is jammed with river weed and stones packed into the paddles, tight as mortar.
prose: They went and looked. The race was the stone channel that brought the river to the wheel, and it was full. Weed was packed into it, long green river weed in wet ropes, wound round and round the paddles. In among the weed were stones, round grey river stones as big as fists and bigger, jammed between the paddles so tight that the paddles couldn't move. Elsie crouched on the bank and pushed at one. It didn't shift. They had been packed in so closely and so neatly, stone on stone with weed between, that it looked like a wall someone had built, tight as mortar.

memory.fact: For a month the Hobb Mill boggart has jammed the wheel with weed and stones every night.

event: Tamsin wades into the race to her waist and hauls stones out, swearing at each one cheerfully.
prose: Tamsin looked at it. She handed Margery to Tilly, who sagged under the weight. She sat on the bank, pulled off her boots, and slid down into the race. The water came up to her waist and she yelled at the cold of it. She waded to the wheel, got her fingers round the first stone, and pulled. It came out with a suck. "There." She slung it up onto the bank. "And stay out." She got hold of the next. "Come here, you lump. Come here, you great ugly— ha!" She swore at each one cheerfully, a different word for every stone, as she hauled them out, and the pile on the bank grew.

event: Tilly passes weed up the bank in armfuls; Elsie, on the sluice, works the slimy stones loose.
prose: Tilly laid Margery down carefully in the grass and came to the edge. Tamsin passed her up the weed in armfuls, great dripping green tangles of it. Tilly took it against her apron and staggered up the bank. She dropped it in a heap and came back for more, soaked to the chest and smelling of river. Elsie went out onto the sluice, the plank walk over the race beside the wheel. She lay on her stomach on the boards and reached down. The top stones were in among the paddles, slimy and green, and she worked them loose with her fingers, wiggling them one way and the other, until each came free in her hand.

event: Cora, coat off and sleeves rolled, takes the stones from Elsie's hands one by one and stacks them.
prose: Cora had taken off her coat. Elsie saw it when she looked up from the sluice, folded on the willow roots, charcoal, with the ledger on top of it. Cora was kneeling at the end of the sluice in her white shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbow. Her forearms were bare and pale, and on one of them was the eel bite Elsie had bandaged, healed now to a pink mark. She held out her hands. Elsie gave her the stone she'd worked loose. Cora took it, wet and green, and set it on a pile beside her. She held out her hands for the next one. They went on like that, stone by stone, from Elsie's hands into Cora's, and Cora stacked them neatly into a little wall of her own.

memory.fact: The eel bite on Cora's forearm has healed to a pink mark.

event: Elsie's hands slip, and Cora catches her wrist and holds it until she has her footing.
prose: A stone came loose all at once. Elsie's hand slid off it on the slime, and her other hand slid off the plank, and she felt herself start to go, head first, over the edge of the sluice toward the race. A hand closed round her wrist. It closed hard and held. It was Cora's. She had come out along the sluice on her knees, and her long fingers went right round Elsie's wrist, tight, on the bare skin above the glove. Elsie scrabbled and found the plank again with her knee, then with her other hand, and got her balance back. Cora held on after that. She held on a while longer, as if she wasn't sure. At last she let go, and sat back on her heels, and held out her hands for the next stone.

event: By three the wheel turns again, and Bess says it'll be choked by morning, it always is.
prose: By three the race was clear. Tamsin slung the last stone up onto the bank and climbed out, streaming. They all stood back. The water came down the race, freed, and struck the paddles, and the wheel groaned. It shook. Slowly, it began to turn. It went round with a long wet creaking, and the water poured off the paddles in sheets and caught the sun. Inside the mill something rumbled awake, and the whole building trembled a little. Tilly cheered. Bess Hobb stood with her arms folded and watched it go round. She didn't cheer. "It'll be choked by morning. It always is."

memory.fact: The party cleared Hobb Mill's race by three on the sixteenth, and the wheel turned again.

event: The younger daughter says it started the week after Gran died, and Bess tells her to hush.
prose:
The younger daughter, the short one, had been standing a little behind her mother with her hands in her apron. "It started the week after Gran died." She was looking straight at Elsie, and it came out fast. "The week after. Not before."

Bess turned on her. "Hush. That's enough." The daughter's mouth went tight. She looked down at her floury boots. But she had said it, and it was out, and Elsie had heard.

event: Elsie asks what Gran used to do of an evening; the daughter says she left cream on the back step.
prose:
Elsie went over to her. "Your gran. What did she use to do? Of an evening, I mean. When the work was done."

The daughter looked at her mother's back. Then she looked at Elsie. "She left cream out." Her voice was low. "Every night. A bowl of cream on the back step, by the wheel, before she went up to bed. She said it kept the wheel sweet." Her chin wobbled. "We used to laugh at her. Mam stopped doing it. After."

memory.fact: Bess Hobb's mother left a bowl of cream on the mill's back step every night, for the wheel.
Bess Hobb's mother left a bowl of cream on the mill's back step every night, for the wheel.

event: Bess says that was Mam's nonsense; Elsie sees her face and says it doesn't sound like nonsense.
prose: Bess spoke loud, to the wheel, without turning round. "That was Mam's nonsense. Cream on a step. Good cream, every night, gone to the cats." But Elsie had come round to where she could see her face. It was red under the flour and set hard. Her mouth was pressed shut, and her eyes were wet. Her chin was going the way her daughter's had. "It doesn't sound like nonsense. It sounds like something she loved doing."

event: Bess sits down on the mill step and cries, once, hard, and Elsie sits by her and holds her hand.
prose: Bess sat down. She sat down on the mill step all at once, as if her knees had given, with her floury hands in her lap. Then she cried. She cried once, hard, one big rough sob that came up out of her like water out of the race, and she put her hands over her face. Elsie sat down beside her on the step. She didn't say anything. She took one of Bess's hands down off her face and held it in both of hers, in her lap, flour and all. It was a big square hand, hard and rough with work, and it gripped hers. They sat like that while the wheel went round, and the daughters stood by.

event: Elsie says the boggart misses Gran too, and might only want thanking; Bess says she'll try it.
prose:
Bess finished at last, and Elsie spoke into the quiet. "I think the boggart misses her too."

Bess looked at her with red eyes.

"Maybe she gave it cream, and it kept the race clear for her. And then the cream stopped. And it doesn't know why." She squeezed the big hand. "Maybe it isn't spite. Maybe it only wants thanking, the way she used to."

Bess looked at the wheel going round for a long while, sniffing. She wiped her nose on the back of her wrist. "I'll try it." It came out gruff. "Tonight. What's a bowl of cream."

event: Supper in the cottage is bread of the mill's own flour and pea soup, and Bess won't take a pip.
prose: Supper was in the cottage at seven, at a long scrubbed table under the thatch, with the door open on the bean rows. There was bread, a big round loaf of the mill's own flour, brown and sweet and still warm in the middle, and a pot of pea soup with mint in it. Tamsin had three bowls. Tilly fell asleep for a moment with her spoon in her hand and woke herself by dropping it. Afterward Elsie took out her purse. Bess looked at it the way the shepherd had. "Put that away. You'll not pay for bread in this house. Not tonight." Elsie put it away.

event: At dusk Bess sets a bowl of cream on the back step by the wheel, and they wait under the willow.
prose: At dusk Bess came out of the dairy with a bowl. It was an old blue bowl, chipped at the rim, and it was full to the brim with thick yellow cream. She carried it to the back step of the mill, by the wheel, and bent, and set it down very carefully on the stone. She stood looking at it a moment with her hands in her apron. Then she came away. They all went and sat under the willow a little way along the bank, Bess and the four of them in a row on its roots, inside the long green curtain of its leaves. They waited. The wheel turned. The sky went from gold to grey. A bat came out over the water.

event: A stone comes out of the dark and cracks against the step; then another, close by Elsie's knee.
prose: It was nearly dark when the first stone came. It came out of the dark on the far side of the race with a whistle and cracked against the step a hand's breadth from the bowl, and bounced into the water. Tilly squeaked. Another came, and hit the willow root right beside Elsie's knee, so close she felt the bark jump under her. It rolled against her boot. She looked down at it. It was a river stone, round and grey and wet, like the ones they'd spent all day pulling out of the race.

event: Tamsin half rises; Elsie puts out a hand and says stay, and Cora shutters her lantern to a thread.
prose: Tamsin was half up off the roots, fast, her hand going for Margery. Elsie put out her hand without looking and laid it flat on Tamsin's arm. "Stay." She kept it very quiet. "Please. It's frightened. Stay." Tamsin stayed. She stayed half crouched, every muscle in her arm tight under Elsie's palm, breathing hard through her nose. On Elsie's other side Cora had her lantern in her lap. She reached down and slid its shutter almost closed, and the light went down to a thread, one thin gold line lying across the grass toward the step.

event: A knee-high hairy thing creeps up the bank to the bowl, eyes like wet pebbles, and drinks.
prose: Something came up the bank. It came out of the water at the foot of the wheel, very slowly, on all fours and then on two. It was small, no higher than Elsie's knee, and covered all over in long brown hair, matted and wet, so that it looked like a heap of weed walking. It had long thin arms and long hands. It stopped. It turned its head toward the willow, and its eyes caught the thread of lamplight, round and dark and shining like wet pebbles in a stream. It went on, to the step, to the blue bowl. It put both long hands round the bowl and bent its face down into it, and drank.

event: Bess, voice cracking, thanks it for keeping the stones out of the race all those years, as Mam did.
prose: Bess stood up. Elsie heard her get up off the roots, slowly, her knees cracking. She didn't go any closer. She stood under the willow with her hands knotted in her apron. "Thank you." Her voice cracked right across the middle. "For the race. For keeping the stones out of it, all those years. Mam always said it was you." She swallowed. "I should've said. I'm sorry. Thank you." The thing at the bowl had lifted its head. It looked at her over the rim, with cream on its whiskers.

event: Elsie says thank you too, very softly, for the wheel and for the flour in her honey cakes.
prose: Elsie got up too, onto her knees on the willow roots. "Thank you." It came out very softly, almost a whisper, so as not to frighten it. "For the wheel. And for the flour." She thought of Mrs Merriweather shaking out the sack, and the honey cakes on the blue plate in the window, and the parcel buttoned inside Noor's coat. "It's in my honey cakes. Your flour. They're very good. So thank you for those as well."

event: The boggart looks at them over the bowl, and between one blink and the next it is gone.
prose: The boggart looked at them over the bowl. It looked at Bess, and at Elsie, with its wet-pebble eyes, a long look, its long hands still round the bowl. Its whiskers dripped. Elsie blinked, and between the blink and the opening of her eyes it was gone. The step was empty except for the blue bowl, licked clean and shining in the thread of lamplight. There was only the sound of the wheel going round. Beside her Tamsin let out a long breath and sat down hard on the roots. Tilly had both hands over her mouth.

prose: Cora slid her lantern shutter open a crack wider. She had put her coat back on. She took the ledger out of it and opened it on her knee and held it to the light. Elsie leaned on her shoulder to watch. Cora wrote the date. She wrote Hobb Mill. She wrote, in her small exact hand, Boggart. Race cleared. Cream on the step. She paused, with the pen lifted, and wrote the line Elsie knew best of all her lines, the one Elsie liked: Skills used, none.

event: Bess gives them the loft over the flour store, sacks for beds and two blankets for four.
prose: Bess gave them the loft over the flour store for the night. It was up a ladder, a long low room under the rafters, warm from the day, smelling of flour and dust and old sacking. Empty sacks were heaped along one wall to sleep on, soft and lumpy. Bess came up the ladder after them with an armful of blankets: two. She looked at the four of them, and at the two blankets, and shrugged. "That's all there is that's dry. You'll manage." She went down again.

event: Tamsin flops on the sacks by the ladder and is snoring like a little kettle in a minute.
prose: Tamsin managed at once. She took the sacks nearest the ladder, flopped down on them face first with her boots still on, pulled one blanket over herself, and in a minute she was asleep. She snored. It was a small, high, bubbling snore, on and on, exactly like a little kettle just coming up to the boil. Tilly giggled. Elsie put a finger to her lips, and giggled too.

event: Tilly takes one blanket with Elsie and curls against her back, her nose in Elsie's hair.
prose: Tilly took the other blanket. She spread it over the sacks along the wall and got under it with Elsie. She lay down at Elsie's back and curled round her, small and warm, her knees fitted in behind Elsie's knees. Her nose went into Elsie's hair, at the nape of her neck. Elsie felt her breathe in there, a long slow breath, and let it out warm against her skin, and do it again. "You smell of honey." It came mumbled into her hair. "And river." Her arm came over Elsie's waist and stayed there.

event: Cora sits against the wall to watch; Elsie says not two nights running, and lifts the blanket.
prose: Cora hadn't lain down. She was sitting against the wall by the little window at the end, knees drawn up, coat on, her lantern beside her shuttered to a thread again, the way she had sat at the barrow. Watching. Elsie lifted her head off the sack. "Cora. No. Not two nights running." She lifted the front edge of the blanket, so there was room in front of her. "Come on. There's space. It's warm." Cora looked at the lifted blanket. She looked at it for a long time.

event: Cora lies down at Elsie's front, very straight, in her shirtsleeves, not quite touching.
prose: Then she got up. She took off her coat and folded it and laid it on the sacks. She took off her boots and set them side by side. She lay down at Elsie's front in her shirtsleeves, on her side, facing her, under the edge of the blanket. She lay very straight. She lay like a ruler, like someone lying to attention, her arms close at her sides, and there was a gap between them, a hand's breadth of warm dark, all the way down. Elsie could feel the warmth of her across it. She wasn't quite touching anywhere.

event: Elsie finds Cora's hands cold again and takes them between hers to warm them.
prose: Elsie found her hands in the dark. They were cold. They were cold the way they had been at the barrow, cold as the morning on the downs, even with the warm loft all round them. She kept her voice to a whisper. "Oh, Cora. Your hands are freezing again." She took them both and folded them between her own, and held them against her chest under the blanket. She rubbed them a little, to bring the warmth back into them. Cora's fingers lay very still in hers. They didn't pull away.

event: She lays her palm flat to Cora's; Cora's fingers are longer by a whole knuckle, and Elsie is glad.
prose: She opened one of the cold hands and laid her own palm flat against it, palm to palm, to see. Cora's fingers went on past the ends of hers, long and thin. They were longer by a whole knuckle. Elsie smiled into the dark. She was glad. She had knitted the glove long in the fingers on purpose, and tried it on her own hand to be sure, and it had flapped at the ends. And here was the proof, cool against her palm, that she had got it right. She pressed their palms together a little and kept her smile to herself.

event: Under Elsie's thumb Cora's pulse is running fast; Elsie thinks she's still cold, and holds on.
prose: She folded her fingers down round Cora's wrist to hold it. Under her thumb, on the soft inside of the wrist, she found Cora's pulse. It was running fast. It was going quick and light and hard against her thumb, as if Cora had run up the ladder instead of lying still. Elsie frowned at it in the dark. Shivering, she thought. She's still cold, right through, from all day in the wet with no coat on. Her poor heart's working to warm her. She held on tighter, and drew Cora's hands closer in against her, and kept her thumb where it was.

event: Cora whispers Fairweather and nothing after it, and Elsie whispers back goodnight, Cora.
prose: "Fairweather," Cora whispered. It was so quiet that Elsie barely heard it over Tamsin's snoring. Elsie waited. There was only the one word. It hung there in the gap between them in the dark, and Cora's breath came after it, warm on Elsie's face, and then she was quiet. Behind Elsie, Tilly sighed in her sleep and burrowed deeper into her hair. "Goodnight, Cora." She squeezed the cold hands.

event: Out in the dark the wheel starts turning again, clear, and Cora's cold hand turns over in Elsie's.
prose: Out in the dark the wheel creaked. Elsie heard it through the loft wall: a long wet groan, a pause, and then the slap of the paddles taking the water again, and the steady pour of it off them, round and round, clear. Under it the river talked over its stones. Elsie lay and listened, with Cora's hands held against her and Tilly's breath in her hair. Between her palms, Cora's cold hand turned over. It turned slowly, until it lay palm up in Elsie's, open, its long fingers resting along the inside of her wrist.
